description:
Wesam Saad continues the evangelism chapter by asking how seriously believers should take Christ’s commission. After reviewing the need for compassion that overcomes fear, he considers the commands to proclaim repentance, make disciples and teach obedience. Matthew 28:18–20 places that mission under Christ’s authority, across all nations and until the end of the age. Wesam therefore argues that the responsibility extends beyond the original apostles. He also connects the beginning and end of Scripture with God’s desire for a people who know Him, treating evangelism as central to the church’s life rather than an optional specialist activity.

Accounts involving Philip, Ananias, Peter and Cornelius show, in his argument, God bringing people together while still requiring human messengers to speak. He links prayer, unity and the use of gifts with a church equipped to proclaim the gospel. Care within the congregation and concern for the lost belong together: unity supports the mission rather than replacing it. He calls listeners to speak of Christ within ordinary relationships as well as organised outreach. The closing discussion adds a pastoral qualification about missed opportunities. Selfishness should be confessed, but exhaustion or another genuine responsibility may require a different response; the heart must be examined honestly, case by case.

questions.question: What does Wesam say should overcome fear of evangelism?
questions.answer: He reviews the earlier call to cultivate compassion for the lost, drawing on Paul’s anguish, Jeremiah’s inability to remain silent and Jesus’s repeated concern for Jerusalem. The aim is not merely to suppress embarrassment, but to develop a concern for others that becomes stronger than the fear of rejection.

questions.question: Why does he regard the Great Commission as binding beyond the original apostles?
questions.answer: Wesam points to all nations and Christ’s promise to be with His people until the end of the age. He argues that the original apostles could not themselves complete that geographical and continuing task. Christ’s authority therefore gives the church both confidence and responsibility to continue making disciples.

questions.question: How does he connect evangelism with the beginning and end of Scripture?
questions.answer: Wesam reads the command to fill the earth in Genesis 1:28 in light of God’s desire for godly people, and connects it with the final invitation to receive the water of life. He presents this as a broad biblical pattern supporting the mission to proclaim salvation, rather than as an isolated activity added to church life.

questions.question: Why does he draw attention to the human messengers in Acts?
questions.answer: In the examples involving Philip, Ananias and Peter, Wesam emphasises that God arranges the encounter while a person still communicates the gospel. He uses those accounts to challenge passive reliance on God to do everything without human involvement. Divine initiative and the believer’s responsibility to speak are held together in his argument.

questions.question: What connection does he see between unity, prayer and proclamation?
questions.answer: Wesam highlights Acts accounts in which believers gather with one mind, pray together and are strengthened to speak. He also notes the addition of people being saved. His point is that church unity and edification should prepare a body for witness, rather than become an inward purpose detached from proclaiming Christ.

questions.question: Can involvement in another ministry replace personal concern for evangelism?
questions.answer: Wesam argues that work closely connected with church life does not exempt a believer from speaking of Christ. He applies that point to music, finance and public teaching. His concern is that valuable service should support a gospel-centred life rather than become an excuse for never communicating the message.

questions.question: Does outward witness require neglecting care within the church?
questions.answer: Wesam says the two belong together. He compares unity and edification with the preparation that makes a task possible, and encourages members to use their gifts to support one another. Concern for people already within the congregation does not exclude concern for those who may yet be brought into it.

questions.question: Does a united church receive a guarantee of immediate evangelistic success?
questions.answer: Wesam explicitly distinguishes faithfulness from a pragmatic promise of success. Supporting one another should strengthen witness, but the church’s responsibility is to follow God’s plan faithfully. He places the final transformation of everything at Christ’s return rather than promising that present unity will secure a particular visible result.

questions.question: Is every missed opportunity to evangelise necessarily the same kind of failure?
questions.answer: Wesam answers case by case. He urges honest examination for selfishness or pride, while acknowledging exhaustion and legitimate competing responsibilities. He gives his own scheduled church commitment as an example. He does not excuse habitual comfort-seeking, but neither does he treat every missed opportunity as grounds for church discipline.
